content.title: 2019 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease
content.narrative_summary: The preamble describes how the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) translate scientific evidence into clinical practice recommendations. It outlines the systematic methods used to develop and classify guidelines, ACC/AHA sponsorship without commercial support, and volunteer task force membership representing diverse expertise and regions. It summarizes policies to mitigate bias and conflicts of interest, and introduces a modular guideline format with tables of recommendations, supporting text, flow diagrams or additional tables as needed, and hyperlinked references.

rows.recommendation: Adults who are 40 to 75 years of age and are being evaluated for cardiovascular disease prevention should undergo 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk estimation and have a clinician–patient risk discussion before starting on pharmacological therapy, such as antihypertensive therapy, a statin, or aspirin. In addition, assessing for other risk-enhancing factors can help guide decisions about preventive interventions in select individuals, as can coronary artery calcium scanning.

All adults should consume a healthy diet that emphasizes the intake of vegetables, fruits, nuts, whole grains, lean vegetable or animal protein, and fish and minimizes the intake of trans fats, red meat and processed red meats, refined carbohydrates, and sweetened beverages. For adults with overweight and obesity, counseling and caloric restriction are recommended for achieving and maintaining weight loss.
Adults should engage in at least 150 minutes per week of accumulated moderate-intensity physical activity or 75 minutes per week of vigorous-intensity physical activity.

For adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus, lifestyle changes, such as improving dietary habits and achieving exercise recommendations, are crucial. If medication is indicated, metformin is first-line therapy, followed by consideration of a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor or a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist.
All adults should be assessed at every healthcare visit for tobacco use, and those who use tobacco should be assisted and strongly advised to quit.
Aspirin should be used infrequently in the routine primary prevention of ASCVD because of lack of net benefit.

Statin therapy is first-line treatment for primary prevention of ASCVD in patients with elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels (≥190 mg/dL), those with diabetes mellitus, who are 40 to 75 years of age, and those determined to be at sufficient ASCVD risk after a clinician-patient risk discussion.

Nonpharmacological interventions are recommended for all adults with elevated blood pressure or hypertension. For those requiring pharmacological therapy, the target blood pressure should generally be <130/80 mm Hg.

content.title: 2019 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease
content.narrative_summary: The page contains the Preamble explaining the guideline’s structure, word limits, web supplement, and refers readers online for the full version. It includes Patrick T. O’Gara’s Chair signature and launches Section 1, noting that ASCVD remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, incurring high costs. It reviews suboptimal prevention, Life’s Simple 7, the importance of ideal cardiovascular health, and the guideline’s aim to consolidate existing and new recommendations on aspirin, lifestyle, team-based care, shared decision-making, and social determinants using a modular format. Section 1.1 describes the guideline’s concise evidence-based methodology, including searches of RCTs, meta-analyses, cohort and observational studies, prior ACC/AHA and USPSTF guidance, with detailed evidence tables online.

section_headings: 1.5 Class of Recommendation and Level of Evidence
content.narrative_summary: This page describes the supplemental evidence resources and processes used to develop the guideline, including the role of Avalere Health in managing the Delphi process and systematic literature searches for exercise, physical activity, and cost/value considerations. It outlines the composition of the writing committee and disclosure procedures (see Appendix 2 and online disclosures), the peer review and approval process involving ACC/AHA and other stakeholders (see Appendix 3), and defines the intended scope of the guideline for primary prevention of ASCVD in adults. Finally, it introduces the framework for assigning Classes of Recommendation (COR) and Levels of Evidence (LOE), with detailed criteria referenced in Table 1 and Supplement S1.5-1.

This page presents Table 1, which defines Class I (strong), Class IIa (moderate), Class IIb (weak), and Class III (no benefit/moderate and harm) recommendations with suggested phrasing, alongside Levels of Evidence A (high‐quality), B-R (moderate-quality randomized), B-NR (moderate‐quality nonrandomized), C-LD (limited data), and C-EO (expert opinion). Footnotes clarify that Class of Recommendation (COR) and Level of Evidence (LOE) are determined independently; LOE C does not imply weakness of recommendation; outcomes should be specified; comparative‐effectiveness recommendations require direct comparisons; the methodology for assessing quality is evolving; and list abbreviations used in the table. Section 1.6 lists clinical abbreviations and their meanings, with the list continuing on the next page.

content.title: 2. OVERARCHING RECOMMENDATIONS FOR ASCVD PREVENTION EFFORTS
section_headings: 2. OVERARCHING RECOMMENDATIONS FOR ASCVD PREVENTION EFFORTS
2.1. Patient-Centered Approaches to Comprehensive ASCVD Prevention
content.narrative_summary: These patient-centered recommendations emphasize team-based care delivery, shared decision-making, and the consideration of social determinants of health in primary ASCVD prevention. The supportive text details how multidisciplinary team-based approaches improve risk factor control; describes collaborative clinician–patient discussions of personalized prevention strategies; and outlines tools to assess socioeconomic, cultural, and upstream determinants—such as housing instability, food insecurity, and health literacy—that influence ASCVD outcomes.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Patient-Centered Approaches to Comprehensive ASCVD Prevention

rows.recommendation: 1. A team-based care approach is recommended for the control of risk factors associated with ASCVD (S2.1-1–S2.1-14).
2. Shared decision-making should guide discussions about the best strategies to reduce ASCVD risk (S2.1-15–S2.1-18).
3. Social determinants of health should inform optimal implementation of treatment recommendations for the prevention of ASCVD (S2.1-19–S2.1-25).

continuity.reason: Narrative supportive text ends mid-sentence

content.narrative_summary: The narrative discusses the importance of assessing social determinants of health (e.g., violence, financial strain, housing, food security, social support) in ASCVD prevention, evaluating systems of care factors such as transportation and health service availability. It highlights that socioeconomic disadvantage affects blood pressure and lipid management, that addressing unmet social needs improves prevention efficacy, and that differential cardiovascular outcomes persist by sociodemographic characteristics. Table 2 summarizes these key considerations.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Assessment of Cardiovascular Risk

rows.recommendation: 1. For adults 40 to 75 years of age, clinicians should routinely assess traditional cardiovascular risk factors and calculate 10-year risk of ASCVD by using the pooled cohort equations (PCE) (S2.2-1, S2.2-2).
2. For adults 20 to 39 years of age, it is reasonable to assess traditional ASCVD risk factors at least every 4 to 6 years (S2.2-1–S2.2-3).

3. In adults at borderline risk (5% to <7.5% 10-year ASCVD risk) or intermediate risk (≥7.5% to <20% 10-year ASCVD risk), it is reasonable to use additional risk-enhancing factors to guide decisions about preventive interventions (e.g., statin therapy) (S2.2-4–S2.2-14).

figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Provides example considerations across domains—including cardiovascular risk, diet, exercise, obesity and weight loss, diabetes mellitus, high blood pressure, and tobacco treatment—with recommendations for assessment of psychosocial stressors, health literacy, food access, neighborhood environment, lifestyle counseling, and social support.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis emphasizes that estimating 10-year ASCVD risk guides the intensity of preventive interventions, encourages a heart-healthy lifestyle, and should initiate clinician-patient risk discussions rather than dictate pharmacotherapy. It notes limitations of risk calculators, potential over- or underestimation in certain populations, and the role of additional risk-enhancing factors (e.g., coronary artery calcium scoring) for borderline or intermediate-risk adults. Lifetime risk estimation may be considered for younger adults, and discussions of preventive therapies should be personalized, especially in older adults.

In adults at intermediate risk (≥7.5% to <20% 10-year ASCVD risk) or selected adults at borderline risk (5% to <7.5% 10-year ASCVD risk), if risk-based decisions for preventive interventions (e.g., statin therapy) remain uncertain, it is reasonable to measure a coronary artery calcium score to guide clinician-patient risk discussion (S2.2-15–S2.2-31).

5. For adults 20 to 39 years of age and for those 40 to 59 years of age who have <7.5% 10-year ASCVD risk, estimating lifetime or 30-year ASCVD risk may be considered (S2.2-1, S2.2-2, S2.2-32–S2.2-35).

content.title: 2019 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease
content.narrative_summary: The narrative discusses the value of coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring for reclassifying borderline- or intermediate-risk patients, guiding decisions about statin or aspirin therapy, and its superior discrimination compared with other subclinical imaging markers. It references observational data and the MESA trial showing CAC’s graded association with 10-year ASCVD risk across age, sex, and racial/ethnic groups, and notes that absence of CAC identifies lower-risk individuals for whom preventive interventions may be deferred. The text also mentions risk estimation tools (CHD, MESA, Astro-CHARM) and the consideration of lifetime or 30-year risk estimation in adults aged 20–59 years to reinforce lifestyle recommendations.

rows.recommendation: A diet emphasizing intake of vegetables, fruits, legumes, nuts, whole grains, and fish is recommended to decrease ASCVD risk (S3.1-1–S3.1-11).
Replacement of saturated fat with dietary monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats can be beneficial to reduce ASCVD risk (S3.1-12, S3.1-13).
A diet containing reduced amounts of cholesterol and sodium can be beneficial to decrease ASCVD risk (S3.1-9, S3.1-14–S3.1-16).
As a part of a healthy diet, it is reasonable to minimize the intake of processed meats, refined carbohydrates, and sweetened beverages to reduce ASCVD risk (S3.1-17–S3.1-24).
As a part of a healthy diet, the intake of trans fats should be avoided to reduce ASCVD risk (S3.1-25–S3.1-27).

content.narrative_summary: The page begins with a Synopsis noting that in 2015 approximately 630,000 Americans died from heart disease, of whom 366,000 died from coronary artery disease, and that heart disease deaths rose by 1% in 2015 largely due to obesity. It emphasizes the impact of healthy nutrition on ASCVD risk factors and discusses limitations of randomized trials, highlighting observational evidence on dietary patterns such as sugar, refined grains, trans fats, processed and red meats. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text reviews evidence supporting specific dietary recommendations: 1) plant-based and Mediterranean diets reduce all-cause and cardiovascular mortality with benefits driven by stroke reduction; 2) trans and saturated fats are linked to higher CVD risk, whereas replacing refined carbohydrates with fats may reduce stroke and mortality; 3) sodium reduction lowers BP and cardiovascular events, and high sodium, red meat, and sugar-sweetened beverages increase CVD risk; 4) sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened beverages are associated with higher T2DM and ASCVD risk, and strategies using low-calorie sweeteners may aid in reducing caloric intake.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues narrative from the prior section on dietary patterns, noting the Southern dietary pattern’s association with increased risks of heart disease, stroke, and mortality, the harms of refined grains, sweetened beverages, low-carbohydrate diets rich in animal fat, and trans fats. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Exercise and Physical Activity

rows.recommendation: Adults should be routinely counseled in healthcare visits to optimize a physically active lifestyle (S3.2-1, S3.2-2).

Adults should engage in at least 150 minutes per week of accumulated moderate-intensity or 75 minutes per week of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity (or an equivalent combination of moderate and vigorous activity) to reduce ASCVD risk (S3.2-3–S3.2-8).

For adults unable to meet the minimum physical activity recommendations (at least 150 minutes per week of accumulated moderate-intensity or 75 minutes per week of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity), engaging in some moderate- or vigorous-intensity physical activity, even if less than this recommended amount, can be beneficial to reduce ASCVD risk (S3.2-5, S3.2-6).
Decreasing sedentary behavior in adults may be reasonable to reduce ASCVD risk (S3.2-3, S3.2-9–S3.2-11).

content.title: 4.2. Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
content.narrative_summary: The page introduces the section on adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus, providing a synopsis of T2DM as a metabolic disorder influenced by diet, activity, and weight, and noting its prevalence and associated ASCVD risk. It begins recommendation-specific supportive text detailing evidence for heart-healthy dietary patterns and exercise programs in glycemic control.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus

rows.recommendation: 1. For all adults with T2DM, a tailored nutrition plan focusing on a heart-healthy dietary pattern is recommended to improve glycemic control, achieve weight loss if needed, and improve other ASCVD risk factors (S4.2-1, S4.2-2).

2. Adults with T2DM should perform at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity to improve glycemic control, achieve weight loss if needed, and improve other ASCVD risk factors (S4.2-3, S4.2-4).

3. For adults with T2DM, it is reasonable to initiate metformin as first-line therapy along with lifestyle therapies at the time of diagnosis to improve glycemic control and reduce ASCVD risk (S4.2-5–S4.2-8).

4. For adults with T2DM and additional ASCVD risk factors who require glucose-lowering therapy despite initial lifestyle modifications and metformin, it may be reasonable to initiate a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor or a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonist to improve glycemic control and reduce CVD risk (S4.2-9–S4.2-14).

content.narrative_summary: The narrative text discusses evidence supporting physical activity for individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), highlighting benefits on cardiovascular disease (CVD) outcomes and recommendations for exercise programs. It describes metformin’s mechanism of decreasing hepatic glucose production and increasing insulin sensitivity, reports findings from the UKPDS showing reductions in microvascular and macrovascular complications and mortality, and summarizes meta-analyses and systematic reviews on metformin’s safety and efficacy. It also notes emerging evidence for SGLT-2 inhibitors reducing CVD events in high-risk T2DM patients.

content.title: 4.3. Adults With High Blood Cholesterol
content.narrative_summary: Above the recommendation table, the text discusses that SGLT-2 inhibitors produce a significant reduction in ASCVD events and heart failure, with benefits extending to primary prevention populations. It describes that GLP-1R agonists increase insulin and glucagon production, enhance glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue, decrease hepatic glucose production, and have been shown to reduce ASCVD risk in adults with T2DM who are at high ASCVD risk. It concludes that in patients with T2DM and additional CVD risk factors, initiating these two classes of medications may be reasonable for primary prevention of CVD before presenting the cholesterol recommendations.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Adults With High Blood Cholesterol

rows.recommendation: In adults at intermediate risk (≥7.5% to <20% 10-year ASCVD risk), statin therapy reduces risk of ASCVD, and in the context of a risk discussion, if a decision is made for statin therapy, a moderate-intensity statin should be recommended (S4.3-2–S4.3-9). Adapted from recommendations in the 2018 Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.3-1).

In intermediate risk (≥7.5% to <20% 10-year ASCVD risk) patients, LDL-C levels should be reduced by 30% or more, and for optimal ASCVD risk reduction, especially in patients at high risk (≥20% 10-year ASCVD risk), levels should be reduced by 50% or more (S4.3-2, S4.3-5–S4.3-10). Adapted from recommendations in the 2018 Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.3-1).

In adults 40 to 75 years of age with diabetes, regardless of estimated 10-year ASCVD risk, moderate-intensity statin therapy is indicated (S4.3-11–S4.3-19). Included from recommendations in the 2018 Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.3-1).

In patients 20 to 75 years of age with an LDL-C level of 190 mg/dL (≥4.9 mmol/L) or higher, maximally tolerated statin therapy is recommended (S4.3-2, S4.3-20–S4.3-25). Included from recommendations in the 2018 Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.3-1).

In adults with diabetes mellitus who have multiple ASCVD risk factors, it is reasonable to prescribe high-intensity statin therapy with the aim to reduce LDL-C levels by 50% or more (S4.3-2, S4.3-7). Included from recommendations in the 2018 Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.3-1).

In intermediate-risk (≥7.5% to <20% 10-year ASCVD risk) adults, risk-enhancing factors favor initiation or intensification of statin therapy (S4.3-7, S4.3-26–S4.3-33). Adapted from recommendations in the 2018 Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.3-1).

In patients at borderline risk (5% to <7.5% 10-year ASCVD risk), in risk discussion, the presence of risk-enhancing factors may justify initiation of moderate-intensity statin therapy (S4.3-28, S4.3-35). Adapted from recommendations in the 2018 Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.3-1).

content.title: 2019 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews evidence supporting statin therapy for primary prevention of ASCVD: large randomized trials demonstrate that moderate-intensity statins reduce risk in intermediate-risk patients, while high-intensity regimens achieve ≥50% LDL-C reduction and greater risk reduction. In adults 40–75 years with diabetes (PCE ≥7.5%), moderate-intensity statins lower ASCVD events by ~25% and are indicated for primary prevention. Patients with primary severe hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL) have high ASCVD risk; placebo-controlled and post hoc analyses support use of moderate-to-high intensity or maximally tolerated statin therapy, with high-intensity yielding greater benefit. First ASCVD events in diabetics carry high morbidity/mortality; although moderate-intensity statins are proven, the higher lifetime risk favors high-intensity statin in diabetics with additional risk modifiers. Risk-enhancing factors (e.g., family history of premature ASCVD, primary LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL, elevated hsCRP) help guide treatment in those at intermediate risk.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative elaborates on risk-enhancing factors beyond diabetes that influence thresholds for statin initiation or intensification, including metabolic syndrome, inflammatory diseases, HIV treated with protease inhibitors, elevated lipoprotein(a), triglycerides, non–HDL-C, and apolipoprotein B. It discusses the role of coronary artery calcium (CAC) measurement in intermediate-risk adults to reclassify ASCVD risk—highlighting that CAC ≥100 AU or ≥75th percentile supports statin initiation, whereas CAC scores of zero confer lower 10-year event rates and may warrant delayed therapy with repeat CAC in 5 years if untreated. The text also notes selected lower-risk individuals who may still benefit from statins and emphasizes shared clinician-patient risk discussions.

content.title: 4.4. Adults With High Blood Pressure or Hypertension
section_headings: 4.4. Adults With High Blood Pressure or Hypertension
Recommendations for Adults With High Blood Pressure or Hypertension
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis summarizes that hypertension is the leading modifiable ASCVD risk factor in the U.S., with a prevalence of SBP ≥130 mm Hg or DBP ≥80 mm Hg in 46% of adults, higher in certain racial/ethnic groups and increasing with age. A log‐linear association between BP levels and ASCVD risk was observed, with each 20-mm Hg higher SBP and 10-mm Hg higher DBP doubling the risk of death from stroke, heart disease, or vascular disease. Although relative risk decreases with age, absolute risk increase is greater in older adults. Refer to Figure 4 and the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice Guidelines for algorithmic details.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Adults With High Blood Pressure or Hypertension

rows.recommendation: In adults with elevated blood pressure (BP) or hypertension, including those requiring antihypertensive medications nonpharmacological interventions are recommended to reduce BP. These include: weight loss (S4.4-2–S4.4-5); a heart-healthy dietary pattern (S4.4-6–S4.4-8); sodium reduction (S4.4-9–S4.4-13); dietary potassium supplementation (S4.4-14–S4.4-18); increased physical activity with a structured exercise program (S4.4-3, S4.4-5, S4.4-11, S4.4-19–S4.4-23); and limited alcohol (S4.4-24–S4.4-29).
rows.supporting_text: Adapted from recommendations in the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.4-1).

rows.recommendation: In adults with an estimated 10-year ASCVD risk* of 10% or higher and an average systolic BP (SBP) of 130 mm Hg or higher or an average diastolic BP (DBP) of 80 mm Hg or higher, use of BP-lowering medications is recommended for primary prevention of CVD (S4.4-30–S4.4-38).
rows.supporting_text: Adapted from recommendations in the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.4-1).

rows.recommendation: In adults with confirmed hypertension and a 10-year ASCVD event risk of 10% or higher, a BP target of less than 130/80 mm Hg is recommended (S4.4-33, S4.4-39–S4.4-42).
rows.supporting_text: Adapted from recommendations in the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.4-1).

rows.recommendation: In adults with hypertension and chronic kidney disease, treatment to a BP goal of less than 130/80 mm Hg is recommended (S4.4-43–S4.4-48).
rows.supporting_text: Adapted from recommendations in the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.4-1).

rows.recommendation: In adults with T2DM and hypertension, antihypertensive drug treatment should be initiated at a BP of 130/80 mm Hg or higher, with a treatment goal of less than 130/80 mm Hg (S4.4-33, S4.4-47, S4.4-49–S4.4-54).
rows.supporting_text: Adapted from recommendations in the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.4-1).

rows.recommendation: In adults with an estimated 10-year ASCVD risk <10% and an SBP of 140 mm Hg or higher or a DBP of 90 mm Hg or higher, initiation and use of BP-lowering medication are recommended (S4.4-36, S4.4-55–S4.4-58).
rows.supporting_text: Adapted from recommendations in the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.4-1).

rows.recommendation: In adults with confirmed hypertension without additional markers of increased ASCVD risk, a BP target of less than 130/80 mm Hg may be reasonable (S4.4-59–S4.4-62).
rows.supporting_text: Adapted from recommendations in the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice Guidelines (S4.4-1).

content.narrative_summary: Recommendation-specific supportive text details evidence for nonpharmacological interventions to lower BP and achieve goal BP, meta-analyses and RCTs supporting BP-lowering medications for ASCVD prevention (including SPRINT trial), and considerations for adults with diabetes mellitus and CKD, noting some trials were underpowered to detect CVD differences.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative continues meta-analytic evidence on blood pressure (BP) targets: bullet 5 discusses initiating antihypertensive therapy in adults with diabetes mellitus and ≥10% ASCVD risk at BP ≥130/80 mm Hg to achieve <130/80 mm Hg, citing RCTs and meta-analyses. Bullet 6 describes a continuous relationship between systolic BP and cardiovascular disease risk across absolute risk levels, with consistent relative risk reductions from BP-lowering medications, and notes the HOPE-3 trial showed no short-term benefit in a lower-risk population.

content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis describes tobacco use as the leading preventable cause of disease and death in the U.S., notes increased mortality and ASCVD risk from smoking, smokeless tobacco, and secondhand smoke, and mentions electronic nicotine delivery systems (e-cigarettes) as a new risk factor with potential cardiovascular effects. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text cites the U.S. Public Health Service’s clinical practice guideline endorsing recording tobacco use as a vital sign, discusses office‐wide screening approaches to facilitate cessation, and recommends specific patient questions to improve disclosure.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Treatment of Tobacco Use

rows.recommendation: 1. All adults should be assessed at every healthcare visit for tobacco use and their tobacco use status recorded as a vital sign to facilitate tobacco cessation (S4.5-1).
2. To achieve tobacco abstinence, all adults who use tobacco should be firmly advised to quit (S4.5-2).
3. In adults who use tobacco, a combination of behavioral interventions plus pharmacotherapy is recommended to maximize quit rates (S4.5-2, S4.5-3).
4. In adults who use tobacco, tobacco abstinence is recommended to reduce ASCVD risk (S4.5-4, S4.5-5).
5. To facilitate tobacco cessation, it is reasonable to dedicate trained staff to tobacco treatment in every healthcare system (S4.5-1).
6. All adults and adolescents should avoid secondhand smoke exposure to reduce ASCVD risk (S4.5-6).

content.title: 2019 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease
content.narrative_summary: This page continues guidance on tobacco cessation assessment and treatment. It describes how clinicians should ask patients about tobacco use—specifically using questions about use in the past 30 days rather than directly “Are you a smoker?”—and strongly advise all tobacco users to quit using clear, compassionate, personalized language. It emphasizes that smoking cessation advice increases quit rates at six months, outlines the benefits of quitting on ASCVD outcomes, and recommends tailoring treatment strategies to individual patient preferences and medical history. The narrative notes expert consensus recommendations (referencing prior sections and Table 8), the removal of FDA black box warnings for neuropsychiatric events, and discusses the substantial net benefit of behavioral interventions and pharmacotherapy in nonpregnant adults and behavioral interventions in pregnant women, while stating that evidence is insufficient to determine the balance of benefits and harms of pharmacotherapy in pregnancy. The text is cut off, indicating continuation on the next page.

content.narrative_summary: Continuation of the tobacco treatment section: ENDS not recommended due to unclear benefit and potential harm; cigarette smoking remains a strong independent risk factor for ASCVD with benefits of cessation; tobacco dependence is a chronic disease requiring trained treatment specialists; secondhand smoke exposure causes CVD and stroke with no safe exposure limit; recommendations to advise patients on exposure precautions. Introduction of section 4.6 on Aspirin Use with a summary table of primary prevention recommendations.

rows.recommendation: 1. Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg orally daily) might be considered for the primary prevention of ASCVD among select adults 40 to 70 years of age who are at higher ASCVD risk but not at increased bleeding risk (S4.6-1–S4.6-8).
2. Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg orally daily) should not be administered on a routine basis for the primary prevention of ASCVD among adults >70 years of age (S4.6-9).
3. Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg orally daily) should not be administered for the primary prevention of ASCVD among adults of any age who are at increased risk of bleeding (S4.6-10).

content.title: 2019 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease
content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis outlines that aspirin is well established for secondary ASCVD prevention but its use in primary prevention remains controversial due to uncertain balance between thrombosis prevention and bleeding risk. It reviews variation among international guidelines and notes recent primary-prevention trials showing less benefit when used alongside modern ASCVD therapies. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text describes meta-regression analyses indicating baseline-estimated ASCVD risk predicts benefit, identifies bleeding-risk scenarios (eg, age >70, prior gastrointestinal bleeding, coagulopathy), and discusses patient-specific factors (eg, weight, risk thresholds) and dose considerations, including low-dose versus high-dose aspirin and trial findings such as from ASCEND.

content.narrative_summary: This page continues discussion of aspirin use for primary prevention of ASCVD, noting insufficient evidence to recommend routine low-dose aspirin in adults under 40 or over 70 years and identifying conditions that increase bleeding risk where prophylactic aspirin should be avoided. It then introduces Section 5 on cost and value considerations, defining value in healthcare, describing methodological challenges in integrating cost–value assessments into guideline development (including variability in costs, benefits, and burden across stakeholders), and highlighting the need for evidence-based, cost-effectiveness analyses of preventive therapies. A block quote from the 2011 AHA policy statement underscores difficulties in assessing long-term prevention value. Section 6 begins by stating most ASCVD events are avoidable through primordial prevention and traditional risk control, but the sentence cuts off.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of lifestyle modifications for primary prevention of ASCVD, emphasizing tobacco avoidance; regular brisk physical activity; a healthy dietary pattern rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, fish, legumes, and poultry; and minimizing trans fats, added sugars, red meats, sodium, and saturated fats. Clinicians should partner with patients to assess readiness for sustained lifestyle improvements, identify barriers, set measurable goals, and monitor progress, while accounting for social determinants of health, health literacy, and motivation. The guideline’s goal is to help clinicians reduce patients’ ASCVD risk and encourage needed healthier lifestyle changes.
